passage:
Session note, Thursday.
Ishita arrived calmer than last month. Her brother Divyansh forgot to collect her after her minor surgery on Saturday; she waited ninety minutes at the hospital gate. In March, she told me, a similar lapse led her to block his number for a week.
This time she described it differently. "He's the one who sat with Amma every night when she was ill. And he forgot me on Saturday. Both are true. I'm allowed to be annoyed, and he's still my brother." She said she told him plainly that the wait hurt; he apologised and cooked dinner for her twice this week.
I pointed out how much steadier this felt than March. Next: we will practise the same both-and phrasing for her conflicts at work.

qa.q: How long did Ishita wait at the hospital gate?
qa.a: Ninety minutes.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling about Divyansh this time?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and hurt about the wait but still affectionate, keeping both his care for Amma and his lapse in view.

qa.q: What does the counsellor plan next, and why?
qa.a: Practising the same both-and phrasing for conflicts at work, because keeping both sides in view made Ishita's reaction steadier than in March.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have experienced the difference from March?
qa.a: Instead of being blocked for a week, he heard plainly that the wait hurt, which gave him the chance to apologise and make amends by cooking dinner.

grounding: An adult tells herself her brother is both caring and careless, and her disappointment stays steady instead of explosive.

passage:
"Tap, tap, tap. Who's coming?" Ganga called from the kitchen.
"Dr Aparna!" Aparna shuffled in wearing Papa's big slippers, a toy stethoscope round her neck. "Open your mouth, please, Amma. Say aaah."
Ganga, grinding coconut for the Onam sadya, opened wide. "Aaah."
"Hmm. Too much payasam," Aparna said, frowning exactly like Papa at his clinic. "Drink water and rest. Next patient!"
"Doctor, will you come to the sadya?"
"Doctors are very busy." Aparna clopped away in the slippers, then peeked back. "But I can come for ten minutes."

qa.q: What was Aparna wearing?
qa.a: Papa's big slippers and a toy stethoscope round her neck.

qa.q: Why does Aparna frown exactly like Papa?
qa.a: She admires Papa 😊, and copying his doctor frown makes her feel big, important and safe.

qa.q: How could Ganga support this kind of play?
qa.a: Keep playing along as the patient and ask about Dr Aparna's work, letting her try on the grown-up role.

qa.q: What is it like for Ganga to be Aparna's patient?
qa.a: She enjoys it, playing along while busy with the sadya, and seems amused to see Papa's frown on her daughter's face.

grounding: A young child wears her father's slippers and copies his doctor's frown and phrases, feeling big like him.

passage:
"Sachin, why are you standing like that?" Deepak asked, leaning on the bat at the colony ground. It was the last week of the summer holidays and dust was everywhere.
"This is how the Captain stands. Bat up, collar up." Sachin flicked his hair, freshly cut into a spike like the poster on his wall.
"Okay, fine. But why did you just tell Vinay he bowls like a grandmother?"
"The Captain says that to bowlers. It's mind games."
"Vinay's nine and it's his first match, yaar."
Sachin paused, still holding the pose. "The Captain also practises four hours every day."
"Copy that part, then. And say sorry to Vinay."

qa.q: What was Sachin's hairstyle like?
qa.a: Freshly cut into a spike like the poster on his wall.

qa.q: Why does Sachin stand with his bat up and collar up?
qa.a: He admires the Captain, and copying the stance makes him feel a little of the hero's strength and confidence.

qa.q: What advice does Deepak give, and why is it good?
qa.a: Copy the Captain's four hours of practice, not the teasing, and say sorry to Vinay 👍; keep the useful value and drop the swagger.

qa.q: How might Vinay feel about Sachin's "mind games"?
qa.a: Vinay, playing his first match, probably felt hurt and nervous at being told he bowls like a grandmother.

grounding: A child copies a cricket hero's stance, hairstyle and taunts, taking in both the hard work and the swagger.

passage:
The school bus was stuck in a January fog jam, forty minutes late, and everyone was restless. Last year, on this same bus, Shalini had been "Chashmish", the girl whose glasses got snatched and passed around. This term she had moved to the back seat with the loud group.
When Gautam, a small Class 8 boy, climbed on with his oversized tiffin bag, Shalini called out, "Here comes the walking suitcase!" The back seat roared. She felt a rush, like finally being on the safe side of the laugh.
Gautam hunched over his bag, ears red, and stared at the fogged window. For a second Shalini saw herself there last year, clutching her glasses. She looked away and laughed louder.

qa.q: What did Shalini call Gautam?
qa.a: "The walking suitcase".

qa.q: What did Shalini feel when the back seat laughed?
qa.a: She felt a rush of relief and power, like finally being on the safe side of the laugh, with a flash of guilt when she remembered herself last year.

qa.q: What could help break this pattern?
qa.a: Shalini could act on that flash of recognition, stop and apologise to Gautam, and a teacher or bus attendant could step in and support both students.

qa.q: What is the bus ride like for Gautam?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and alone, hunching over his bag with red ears, just as Shalini once felt.

grounding: A teenager who was once mocked on the bus starts mocking a smaller student, taking the powerful role and passing on the harm.

subtype: Absorbing a mentor's way of speaking [Actor]
passage:
It was peak wedding season, and the hotel kitchen in Amritsar had three receptions in one night. Amandeep, six months into his traineeship, found himself shouting "Clean station, clean mind!" exactly the way Chef Naveen did, clapping twice after each order. He even tucked a pen behind his left ear like Naveen. It worked: the junior cooks listened, and Amandeep felt taller.
Around midnight, though, the double clap made a nervous new trainee drop a tray of rotis. Amandeep caught himself. The clap was Naveen's; on Amandeep it felt like borrowed armour. On the next order he simply said, "Two dal, two paneer, let's go, I'm right here," and stood beside the trainee. That felt more like him. He kept the line about clean stations.

qa.q: What phrase did Amandeep shout the way Chef Naveen did?
qa.a: "Clean station, clean mind!"

qa.q: Why did copying Naveen's habits make Amandeep feel taller?
qa.a: He felt more confident borrowing the style of a senior he admired, especially under the pressure of three receptions in one night.

qa.q: What did Amandeep learn about which habits to keep?
qa.a: To test each habit: the clean-station line fits him, but the clap frightened a new trainee, so he swapped it for a calmer style of his own.

qa.q: How did the nervous trainee experience the clapping?
qa.a: The trainee was startled and dropped a tray of rotis, feeling more pressure instead of guidance.

grounding: A young trainee copies a senior chef's phrases and habits to feel confident, then tests which ones really fit him.

subtype: Choosing which parental traits to keep [Response]
passage:
In the family cloth shop in Kurukshetra, Vaibhav was counting the day's cash when Mehak, the new helper, folded a stack of dupattas crookedly. "Is this how you fold? Did no one teach you anything?" he snapped.
Mehak's face fell. Vaibhav froze. That was Pitaji's voice, word for word. He remembered standing in this same shop at twelve, hands shaking over a crooked fold. He remembered too that Pitaji raised the shutter at seven every single day and knew every customer's name.
Vaibhav put the notes down. "Sorry, Mehak. That came out harsh. Let me show you the fold." He did, slowly, twice.
That night he wrote on the back of a bill: Keep: seven o'clock, every name. Drop: the tone.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav write on the back of the bill?
qa.a: "Keep: seven o'clock, every name. Drop: the tone."

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he froze after snapping?
qa.a: He felt shocked and ashamed to hear his father's sharp voice in his own mouth, remembering how scared he had been in the shop as a boy.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Apologising, showing the fold slowly, and writing down which of Pitaji's habits to keep and which to drop turned an inherited reflex into a deliberate choice.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel after Vaibhav's apology?
qa.a: Relieved and more at ease, since the harsh words were taken back and she was shown the fold patiently.

grounding: A young shopkeeper hears his strict father's voice in himself and chooses to keep the diligence and drop the sharpness.

passage:
Dear Diary, Friday, rainy (monsoon, again)
Yesterday I called Irawati "Iron-teeth" because she wouldn't let me see her maths answers. Everyone laughed and she went quiet all afternoon.
Today I gave her my best sticker, the shiny rocket one, and said, "Here, you can have this." I didn't say anything else. She said "thanks", but she didn't smile like normal. She stuck it on her bottle anyway.
I thought the sticker would make it fine. Like rubbing out a wrong answer. But it still feels a bit wrong. Mummy says sorry is just one word. Maybe tomorrow I will say it.
Kunal

qa.q: Which sticker did Kunal give Irawati?
qa.a: The shiny rocket one, Kunal's best sticker.

qa.q: Why did Kunal give the sticker without saying anything about the name?
qa.a: Kunal felt guilty 😔 and hoped the gift would rub out the hurt, like erasing a wrong answer, without the awkwardness of saying sorry.

qa.q: What would finish the job?
qa.a: Saying sorry for "Iron-teeth" out loud, so Irawati knows it was wrong and not just covered over.

qa.q: How does Irawati seem to feel about the sticker?
qa.a: She accepts it politely but does not smile like normal, suggesting she is still hurt and needs the words.

grounding: A child who called a friend a name gives a sticker the next day without mentioning it, and senses an apology is still needed.

passage:
So, Diwali week, right? Everyone's cleaning. Papa asked me three times to sort my cupboard, and the third time I just yelled, "Can you stop controlling my life?" Loud. The neighbours definitely heard. He didn't say anything, just went out to the balcony.
And then I felt awful. So I cleaned. Not just my cupboard. The whole kitchen, the fans, even the steel dabbas. Then I made him ginger tea, exactly how he likes it, and left it next to him. Didn't say a word.
He drank it. He even said, "Good tea, Usha." But at dinner he was still quiet. My friend asked if I'd said sorry, and I was like, I cleaned the fans! Isn't that sorry? But maybe he needed to hear it. Maybe I'll say it tonight.

qa.q: What kind of tea did Usha make for Papa?
qa.a: Ginger tea, exactly how he likes it.

qa.q: Why did Usha clean the whole house after yelling?
qa.a: Usha felt guilty and awful about the outburst, and cleaning and making tea were a way to show regret without having to say it.

qa.q: What could Usha add to the cleaning and the tea?
qa.a: A simple spoken sorry that names the yelling 🙏, so Papa hears the apology and does not just see it.

qa.q: What might Papa need after being yelled at?
qa.a: He was probably hurt; the tea touched him, but his quiet dinner suggests he still needs to hear an actual sorry.

grounding: A teenager who yelled at a parent cleans the house and makes tea in silence, the actions showing guilt that still needs words.

passage:
At the Christmas party in our hostel common room, Tejas made a joke about my accent in front of everyone: "Kunal, say 'financial' again, please, for the village people." The room laughed. I laughed too, then left early.
Two days later, just before the winter break, he handed me a box. Wireless earbuds, the expensive kind. He smiled as if nothing had happened. "Merry Christmas."
I stood there holding the box, feeling strangely worse. It was like he was paying to delete the evening.
I didn't want to be rude. So I said, "This is really generous, thank you. But honestly, I'd rather talk about the party. That joke stung." He went red, then sat down on my bed. "Yeah. It was a cheap shot. Sorry."
I kept the earbuds. The talk mattered more.

qa.q: What gift did Tejas give Kunal?
qa.a: Wireless earbuds, the expensive kind.

qa.q: Why did Kunal feel worse holding the gift?
qa.a: Kunal felt hurt and a bit resentful, sensing that the gift and smile were trying to wipe away the insult without any talk.

qa.q: What did Kunal do that worked?
qa.a: Thanking Tejas kindly but saying a talk mattered more, and naming the joke that stung, led to a real apology.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling when he handed over the box?
qa.a: Tejas probably felt guilty about the joke but found a gift easier than words; going red shows his embarrassment once it was named.

grounding: A student mocked at a party receives an expensive gift instead of an apology, and kindly asks to talk instead.

subtype: Overworking to make up for a mistake [Actor]
passage:
Carnival week in Recife meant half the office was out dancing, but Priscila stayed at her desk until ten every night. Three weeks earlier she had missed the deadline for the port authority report, and the client had been furious. Since then she had redone every chart twice, answered emails at midnight and skipped lunch.
When Jin offered to check the appendices, she snapped, "No. It was my mistake, I'll fix it." Her eyes were ringed with shadows, and she had started forgetting small things, like her coat.
On Friday, Jin left a note on her keyboard: "The client already accepted the revised report. You don't owe anyone more nights." Priscila read it twice, then sat back, too tired to argue.

qa.q: Which report did Priscila miss the deadline for?
qa.a: The port authority report.

qa.q: Why did Priscila refuse Jin's help?
qa.a: She felt guilty about the missed deadline and believed she had to fix it alone, as if extra suffering could erase the error.

qa.q: What would cost Priscila less than weeks of late nights?
qa.a: Simply owning the mistake, accepting help like Jin's, and going home once the revised report was accepted.

qa.q: How does Jin see Priscila's late nights?
qa.a: Jin is concerned, noticing her tiredness and forgetfulness, and gently points out that the client has already accepted the report.

grounding: An employee who missed a deadline works late for weeks and refuses help, trying to erase the mistake through penance.
